strengths: Comprehensive and well-organized experimental pipeline spanning encoding, decoding, generative modeling, and behavioral/cognitive analysis across two large datasets (HCP N=1067; BSNIP N=984), with consistent subject-wise splits and repeated seeds/5-fold CV.

Careful leakage prevention: the Procrustes gradient template is derived strictly from the resting-state training set, parcellations are learned only from training subjects, and normalization statistics are train-only. This is more rigorous than much of the connectome ML literature and is explicitly documented.

The central claim that aligned functional gradients act as a useful inductive bias is directly supported by targeted ablations (aligned vs. unaligned gradients, edge-only, graph-theoretic features, constant features) across parcellations and rest/task settings, and the four-structure ablations (alignment, edge conditioning, memory, node features) isolate each design choice.

Evaluation goes beyond reconstruction: latent linear separability of tasks and clinical groups, reduced-rank readouts of latent structure, behavior regression controlling for age/gender with FDR correction, and generative validation in both latent space (MMD, 1-NN two-sample) and graph space (KS statistics on weights, leading eigenvalues, clustering, modularity, small-worldness).

Reasonable, adaptable baselines (GAE, Graphite, GRALE, GATE, GraphMAE, FC+UMAP) with matched latent dimensionality and node features for fairness, plus per-step runtime profiling; the appendix provides enough hyperparameter detail to be largely reproducible.

Honest and specific limitations section (fixed parcellation/correspondence, quadratic attention cost, gradient estimation dependence on preprocessing, cross-site generalization) and a thoughtful impact statement covering cohort bias, clinical over-interpretation, and privacy of embeddings.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is largely an assembly of existing components (edge-conditioned attention from Ma et al. 2023, diffusion-map gradients, memory-based cross-attention decoding, DDPM on latents). The contribution is connectome-specific integration rather than a new learning principle, which narrows its interest for the main ICML track.

Reconstruction gains over the strongest baselines are modest in absolute terms (e.g., 0.0124 vs. 0.0155 for GATE at rest) and no statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are provided for baseline comparisons; the paper does not establish whether MSE differences are robust to the confound that MSE on dense, low-rank FC can be driven largely by predicting the global mean connectivity pattern rather than subject-specific edge structure.

Clinical decoding results are weak and under-analyzed: BSNIP HC vs. SCZ accuracy (0.6646) and AUC (0.7370) are barely above the baselines and carry large variance across folds (±0.05–0.10); no confidence intervals or significance tests are given, yet this is presented as evidence of functional meaningfulness.

Behavioral associations have small effect sizes (βdisp = 0.08–0.15, r = 0.23) with multiple comparisons across tasks and metrics; the narrative interpretation (e.g., linking dispersion to intelligence via neural efficiency) is speculative relative to the evidence, and causality-free correlational claims are stated somewhat strongly.

The generative model is evaluated only via distributional statistics (MMD, KS, 1-NN); there is no demonstration of downstream utility of synthetic connectomes (e.g., augmentation improving a classifier, or biological plausibility checks by neuroscientists), so the practical value of the diffusion component remains unproven.

The introduction motivates dense attention via over-smoothing and sparse-attention risks, but these claims are not tested (no MPNN over-smoothing baseline, no sparse-attention comparison); the argument is asserted rather than empirically supported.

Several presentation/reproducibility gaps: the code availability and citation lines contain blank URLs ('Code is available at .'), Figure 6 axis labels in the appendix are unreadable, and the neural-dynamics extension's added value over the spatial model is reported only for one dataset with no ablation of the fusion mechanism itself.

Only one parcellation family and one atlas are used; given that all conclusions hinge on the gradient-alignment inductive bias, sensitivity to atlas choice is claimed as a limitation but not explored even briefly.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: learning unsupervised, graph-level representations of dense, weighted functional connectomes without thresholding addresses a real gap in connectome ML, and the motivation for using functional gradients (aligned diffusion-map embeddings) as a domain-specific inductive bias is clearly argued.

Careful experimental hygiene: the gradient template is derived strictly from the resting-state training set to avoid leakage (Section 2.1), coarse parcellations are derived from training subjects only (Appendix A), node features are normalized with training-set statistics, and downstream classifiers are fit post-hoc on frozen embeddings under subject-wise splits. This is more rigorous than typical connectome deep learning papers.

Comprehensive evaluation: reconstruction and downstream classification across multiple baselines (GAE, Graphite, GRALE, GATE, GraphMAE, FC+UMAP) and ablations (no alignment, no edge conditioning, no memory, edge-only) across three parcellation resolutions (Tables 1-2), plus latent-space diagnostics (Fig. 2B-C, reduced-rank regression), generation validation in both latent and graph space (Fig. 4), and behavioral associations with covariate and FDR controls (Section 3.3).

Good reproducibility: full hyperparameters, training protocol, computational cost comparison, baseline adaptation details (Appendix C-D), and a code release are provided. The impact statement and limitations section are honest and substantive.

Interesting scientific finding: directional (PC2, gradient-related) task reconfiguration is positively associated with composite cognition while global dispersion is negatively associated, which is a nuanced, interpretable result (Fig. 3).
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the paper is largely an assembly of existing components - edge-conditioned transformer attention from Ma et al. (2023), attention pooling, a memory-based cross-attention decoder, and a standard DDPM prior on latents. The core contribution is applying and tuning these to dense FC, which may be seen as domain engineering rather than a general methodological advance for ICML.

Statistical rigor of comparisons is incomplete: MSE and accuracy differences over baselines are reported as mean ± SD over four seeds, but no significance tests or confidence intervals on the differences are provided. Several gaps are small (e.g., BSNIP AUC 0.737 vs GATE 0.658, with SD ~0.05, and reconstruction MSE 0.0124 vs 0.0155), so it is hard to judge whether the headline improvements are reliable.

The cognitive-decoding gains from the temporal extension (Section 3.2.3) are somewhat trivially expected: RNNs operating on task-block time series directly observe stimulus-locked dynamics, so improved 0-back/2-back and stimulus decoding may reflect information the temporal stream already contains rather than a benefit of the geometry-guided spatial representation. A clearer control (e.g., temporal-only model) is needed to attribute the gain to the fused geometry.

Generation evaluation lacks generative baselines: the diffusion prior is compared only against the empirical distribution (MMD, 1-NN, KS statistics); no comparison to simpler generative models (e.g., Gaussian fit, VAE, GAN, or direct matrix-space diffusion) is provided, making it unclear that latent diffusion is the right choice for FC generation.

The central 'low-dimensional latent geometry along which topology and spectra vary smoothly' claim is supported mainly by qualitative scatter plots and modest correlations (r = 0.23 for PC2 variance and cognition; two-factor R^2 = 0.52), without formal smoothness metrics or tests of the manifold hypothesis.

The behavioral effects are small (|β| = 0.07-0.23) and derived from a single cohort; the BSNIP clinical classification gains are modest and could reflect cohort confounds (motion, demographics) not fully addressed.

Minor presentation issues: the code availability URL appears blank in Section 3.1 and Appendix E, and some claims (e.g., range(ψk) vs λk correlation) defer entirely to an appendix without inline quantification.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated gap: unsupervised, graph-level representation learning directly from dense, weighted functional connectomes, without the thresholding/sparsification steps that are known to be problematic in network neuroscience (citing Garrison et al., 2015; van Wijk et al., 2010).

The domain-specific inductive bias (aligned diffusion-map functional gradients as node features, with a leakage-free, training-rest-only Procrustes template) is connectome-specific and clearly differentiated from prior geometry-guided graph learning based on structural encodings or external spatial coordinates.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for a domain paper: multiple datasets (HCP N=1067; BSNIP N=984 with 5-fold CV), four seeds for HCP splits, adapted baselines (GAE, Graphite, GRALE, GATE, GraphMAE, FC+UMAP), ablations (no alignment, no edge conditioning, no memory, edge-only), parcellation sensitivity (64/100/150 regions), and gradient-count sensitivity (F in {5,10,20,30}).

Generation quality is validated in both latent space (MMD, 1-NN two-sample test) and graph space (weight distributions, leading eigenvalues, clustering, modularity, small-worldness), which is more rigorous than typical connectome-generation papers.

Reproducibility is strong: full hyperparameters, optimization details, baseline adaptation details, parcellation-construction protocol, computational cost comparison, and code availability are provided in the appendix.

The limitations and impact statement sections are honest and substantive (fixed parcellation constraint, quadratic attention cost, dependence on gradient estimation/alignment, cohort/preprocessing bias, privacy considerations), and the leakage-prevention protocols (train-only gradient template, train-only parcellations, subject-wise splits) are carefully handled.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily at the level of a well-executed domain synthesis rather than a new method: the edge-conditioned transformer encoder follows Ma et al. (2023), the memory-based cross-attention decoder and latent diffusion are standard, and the diffusion-map gradient pipeline is established connectomics practice. The central claim of 'geometry-guided' learning rests on showing alignment + gradients help, which the ablations do support, but the architectural novelty is incremental.

The spatial-temporal fusion claim lacks a dynamics-only control. The 84.5%/75.2% stimulus decoding improvements from fusing neural dynamics are attributed to the fused representation, but there is no GRU-only (temporal, no spatial) baseline, so it is unclear how much of the decoding signal comes from the time series alone versus the geometry-guided spatial pathway.

The behavioral/cognitive findings have small effect sizes (r = 0.23, β = 0.07, |βdisp| = 0.08–0.15). Although FDR-corrected and controlling for age/gender, these correlations are modest and correlational; the interpretation linking dispersion to 'neural efficiency' is plausible but speculative, and the paper appropriately frames this as exploratory.

HC vs. schizophrenia classification on BSNIP (66.5% accuracy, AUC 0.737 ± 0.048) is modest with high variance, and the margin over baselines (e.g., GATE at 0.658) is within roughly one standard deviation, so the claimed advantage on the clinical task is weakly supported.

The fixed-parcellation setting plus the learnable node memory in the decoder make the reconstruction task comparatively easy (node identity is effectively given), which may inflate the apparent advantage over baselines on reconstruction MSE; absolute MSE differences (e.g., 0.0124 vs. 0.0155–0.0177) are small, and no statistical significance tests are reported for the reconstruction comparisons.

Generative evaluation is purely distributional; there is no downstream utility test of generated graphs (e.g., augmentation for classification or training data simulation), which limits the demonstrated significance of the diffusion component.

Some analysis details are deferred to an appendix that is referenced but not included in the reviewed material (e.g., the correlation between range(ψ) and λ, and additional baselines), making several claims in Sections 3.2.2 and 2.1 unverifiable from the main text.
